In terms of working career, I commenced my training with Pricewaterhouse from 1990 and continued working post-qualification with PricewaterhouseCoopers in their UK financial services practice. After various management roles, including leading business divisions, I was promoted to the UK Assurance Executive, where I led the UK's financial services practice.
This was multidisciplinary with multiple stakeholders, and the key priorities were business development across markets, delivering excellent client service, people and talent development, and overall business performance. At PwC, I had the great privilege to work with a very wide range of global and local organizations on their commercial developments, reporting, including financial, management, and regulatory disciplines, M&A, risk management, control frameworks, and change and project agendas.
After I'd been at PwC some 28 years, I commenced working with the asset manager Standard Life Aberdeen, listed on the stock exchange, which was later rebranded Aberdeen plc. They were undertaking significant changes post their merger back in 2017.
From 2019 to 2023, I undertook the role of Executive Director and CFO, undertaking the stewardship of financial and balance sheet management in the UK, in Asia, and in the US, management of shareholder investments, and delivery of investor and regulatory reporting. I am grateful for the trust placed in me by the board, and I hope I can count on your vote today. I will use my financial experience to contribute to Allianz's sustained growth and continued success, and I very much look forward to working with the board. Thank you.
Michael Diekmann
Chairman of the Supervisory Board, Allianz SE
Yes, Mrs. Bruce. It's a particular pleasure for me now that Dr. Schneider can be introduced by me, who's been, you know, serving on the other side of the road from Munich Re. 18 years of that, he worked for that company as CFO. In case that Mr. Schneider that is going to be elected into the Supervisory Board, then he will also be available as Deputy Chairman in the constituting meeting and being suggested as the deputy member of the Supervisory Board. Mr. Schneider.
Jörg Schneider
Former CFO, Munich Re
Thank you very much, Mr. Diekmann, for giving me the opportunity to introduce myself and for you, dear shareholders. Ladies and gentlemen, I am Jörg Schneider. I'm 65 years old, and I studied in business administration. I'm a lawyer. I've been married for 40 years, and we have two children that were given to me and my wife. After my training and dual business administration studies at Daimler-Benz, I studied law, and I wrote a thesis.
Mr. Diekmann said after that Mercedes-Benz career, he summarized everything and not to make it unilateral. For more than 30 years, I worked for Münchener Rück. That is very close here, not only working for Mercedes-Benz. I started in business administration and also in participations for seven years.
Seven years later, I moved up to the Board of Management, and then I assumed the responsibility for credit insurance and our IT department. Then afterwards, like Mr. Diekmann stated, I worked 18 years as CFO with my employees and my team, and we were responsible for accounting, risk management, compliance, controlling, and taking care of the investments and the investors.
After I left the Board of Management of Münchener Rück roughly five years ago, now I've been working in the Supervisory Board of the Bayerische Landesbank and also in the Advisory Board of ALDI SÜD. In both companies, I'm heading the audit committee.
Here at Allianz, in the course of the preparation for my new task during the past few months, I was able to use a lot, and I've seen a lot of things that I knew from my experience, and I learned a lot about that company and the latest market developments. That's why I'm quite confident that I'm able to contribute to the most important topics of Allianz, and being an asset manager, to render my contribution in the Supervisory Board.
I do know from my earlier close cooperation between Münchener Rück and Allianz, and thanks to very good contacts that I still have, that Allianz possesses very good and very potent employees that work with responsibility. That's why it's both an honor and full pleasure that I'm able to work in the Supervisory Board of Allianz, and that's why I kindly ask you to give me your vote and your trust. Thank you so much.
Michael Diekmann
Chairman of the Supervisory Board, Allianz SE
Thank you very much, Mr. Schneider. Both candidates will be suggested for a regular term of four years until the annual meeting in 2028. This will ensure that the Staggered Board introduced in 2022, that is staggered terms of office, are being maintained. With the candidates proposed today, the Supervisory Board of Allianz will continue to be very well-staffed in terms of the expertise expected by the regulators and investors, particularly in the insurance and financial services business, accounting and risk management, as well as experience in managing companies.
The Supervisory Board's proposal also takes into account the requirements of independence and internationality, as well as diversity and the appropriate participation of women. I can also point out that there are no personal or business relationships within the meaning of German Corporate Governance Code between Mrs. Bruce or Dr. Schneider and the Allianz Group, the executive bodies of Allianz SE, or a shareholder with a material interest that would preclude their election into the Supervisory Board.
The new elections will be held in the form of individual elections. You will find detailed CVs for Mrs. Bruce and Dr. Schneider in the invitation to the AGM. I would like to ask you to support the candidates proposed by the Supervisory Board with your vote. This brings me to the end of my report, and I would like to thank you for your attention. I would like to ask Mr. Bäte, the Chairman of the Board of Allianz SE, for his report of the annual general meeting.
Oliver Bäte
Chairman of the Board, Allianz SE
Good morning, ladies and gentlemen, dear shareholders, dear employees. Greetings from Munich. It's raining outside, but we have the sun in our heart, as they like to say here in Munich, and we're looking forward to this day with you. Today, I would like to discuss two topics together with you. How has Allianz developed over the past year, and what does our path into the future look like? Before we address these questions, I would like to take a look back together with you at the year 2023.
After all, we need to assess what we've achieved against the backdrop of the path we've traveled over the course of the last year. Mr. Diekmann already mentioned that the challenges of the past year were enormous once again. We saw how the major economies were still scarred by the crises of recent years.
We saw wars in the middle of Europe and then in the Middle East. We experienced one of the warmest years ever. If, as if that wasn't enough, we lived through a technological revolution. Let me expand on this for a moment. Let's start with the economic development. Here, I would like to start in Germany, but also in the US, inflation was the topic that dominated capital markets and companies and affected every one of us.
No one was spared rising costs. In an unprecedented race, the central banks in the US and Europe raised interest rates up to 5% over just six months, a level that we last saw in the early 2000s. Inflation was thus contained, at least to a large degree.
Nevertheless, especially the German economy suffered that at the end of the year 2023, ladies and gentlemen, Germany was in a recession. The situation was quite different in the US. They had already decided to invest around EUR 370 billion the year before and were thus able to build on their growth before the COVID pandemic.
At the other end of the world, in China, we saw an opposite development. Inflation was the lowest in 10 years, and a key driver was the ongoing crisis in the real estate sector. Countless families in China, for example, lost large parts of their savings.
The construction group, Evergrande, which was heavily indebted at around EUR 300 billion and became a symbol of how trust in an entire industry was lost, a symbol for that was seen all over the world, an industry that had boosted Chinese growth for years. Another contrast. We saw India's boom, which could hardly be greater these days. India recorded the highest growth rates among the world's 10th largest economies.
In just a few years, ladies and gentlemen, India will overtake Germany and Japan as the world's third-largest economy. The key to this is India has invested heavily in education, digitalization, and infrastructure. An example for all of us, we think. At the same time, the crisis in the world has intensified. The war in Ukraine has marked its second anniversary with no end in sight, probably. Western supporters are increasingly divided over further aid.
The smoldering conflict between Israel and Hamas escalated in H2, further destabilizing the region. More than 1 million people in the Gaza Strip in Israel have become refugees through this, and today they live in undignified conditions. As if that was not enough, all of this happened in the warmest year since records began. Climate change is progressing. It's threatening our livelihoods, our homes, and the health of all people.
Last year alone, natural disasters caused damage amounting to around $280 billion again. Ladies and gentlemen, last year we also witnessed a technological revolution. With so-called large language models, we could communicate with AI in our own language for the first time. For example, artificial intelligence can now answer questions in a meaningful way. It can write texts and create translations.
For companies, it opens new potentials in automation, but also in innovation. It is an equalizer in society, as you could say, because it makes skills that were previously acquired only in education now accessible to everyone. Inflation and stagnation in the Western economies, the boom of India, wars on our doorstep, natural disasters, a technical or a technological revolution.
Ladies and gentlemen, the past year once again showed us how much, and above all, how quickly the world we live in is changing. Things that seemed certain yesterday are already changing today, and this dynamic is unsettling many of us. It makes many people afraid of losing their jobs and prosperity, especially in Europe. It also makes some afraid of the future.
We think Allianz, ladies and gentlemen, was founded 134 years ago precisely for this kind of environment, to provide security in uncertain times, to create trust and hope, and to protect what is most important to our customers. Our old advertising slogan, "Hoffentlich Allianz," hopefully insured with Allianz, is therefore more relevant today than ever. What does this mean, ladies and gentlemen, in concrete terms? What does it mean for each and every one of us?
For this, I would like to tell you the story of our customer, Elfriede Carrel. A story about how the worst befell her during the most beautiful time of the year, and how we did everything we could to bring her home again safely. After a long working life, Mrs. Carrel and her husband have fulfilled their dream of spending part of the year in warm and sunny Florida.
This was also the case last spring when she was bitten by an insect there. Not a big deal, she thought, but what she didn't know was that from that moment on, a race against time had started, a race for her life. Because that sting transmitted a bacterium that destroys the skin and surrounding tissue. The disease spreads rapidly, at lightning speed, and if left untreated, it can be fatal within a few days.
Mrs. Carrel's condition deteriorated fast, and her husband took her to the emergency room that very evening. The doctors, thank God, immediately recognized the dramatic nature of the situation, and they removed the diseased tissue that very night. Exhausted and unsettled, our customer's husband contacted us the next morning. He was looking for advice and wanted to get home to his family with his wife as quickly as possible.
Our emergency doctor of Allianz, Julia Greipel, got in touch immediately. She consulted with the doctors in the US and arranged for the treatment at a specialist hospital in Heidelberg. There, close to her family, Mrs. Carrel was to recover from her illness. Ms. Greipel then traveled to the US herself and accompanied the Carrel couple on their journey home. Thank God, Mrs. Carrel has now left the hardships behind her, and she's infinitely grateful for the support she received from your Allianz.
Now, why am I telling you this story, ladies and gentlemen? Because it's precisely these moments that count. We were there for a customer when the worst befell her. We stood by her, and we gave confidence and brought her home safely. In these very moments, our commitment to protecting what is most important to our customers becomes tangible, in this case, her health.
Ladies and gentlemen, an annual general meeting is a moment to review and a moment in which we can show that you've rightly placed your trust in us as a company. I'm very pleased that I once again have a lot of good news to report at this point, by the way, for the 10th time as your CEO. Last year, we consolidated our position as one of the world's leading insurers and asset managers.
Our revenue reached EUR 162 billion, an increase of 5.5% year on year. The operating profit increased once again by 6.7% to EUR 14.7 billion, a record value. Our core return on equity rose to a strong 16%, and the shareholders' core net income amounted to EUR 9.1 billion, an increase of around 30%.
Let us now briefly touch upon the individual segments. In Property-Casualty insurance, we increased our revenues by 8.4%. We achieved around EUR 77 billion in revenues. The operating profit, for the first time, exceeded EUR 6.9 billion. We also grew in Life and Health insurance. The value of new business rose by 2.2% to EUR 4 billion, and the operating profit of EUR 5.2 billion shows our high earning power.
In Asset Management, we once again held our ground in a difficult market. We achieved an operating profit of EUR 3.1 billion, and we increased our third-party assets under management by around EUR 77 billion to EUR 1.7 trillion.
We achieved these very strong results despite the enormous challenges we faced last year, because, for example, in Property-Casualty insurance, inflation was clearly reflected in repair costs. This development was driven above all by higher wages and also due to more repairs of electric cars. We again had to cope with higher claims for more frequent and more severe natural disasters.
The capital markets were also tighter than ever last year. On the one hand, shares and bonds rose significantly over the course of the year. The end of the year in particular saw a rally in stock markets worldwide. On the other hand, the collapse, as you might remember, of three regional banks in the US shook confidence in the financial sector. The situation was exacerbated by the takeover of Credit Suisse by UBS in Switzerland.
Many investors feared a contagion similar to the banking crisis of 2008, but luckily it didn't come to this. Now, how have we developed? With our high financial strength, we were able to remain steady in this environment. The leading rating agencies count us amongst their top group. Ladies and gentlemen, that is what we are once again increasing our dividend to do.
You will benefit from a dividend amounting to 60% of our surplus, which is an increase of 10 percentage points compared to a previous payout ratio. We aim to continue to pay at least the dividend of the last year. Already this year, we therefore plan for a dividend of EUR 13.80 per share, which is a significant increase of 21% compared to the last year.
By the way, with that, we are increasing our dividend for the seventh time in eight years. Moreover, last year, we bought back shares for around EUR 2 billion. As a result, you achieved an excellent total return of 27%. This is one of the best results in our sector. We've already announced share buybacks of over EUR 1 billion for the current year. Ladies and gentlemen, also that contributes to the fact that our share is the most popular share amongst private investors in Germany.
What's important for me personally, more than 112,000 Allianz employees are also shareholders today, which is 70% of our workforce approximately. Just to compare, in 2018, so six years ago, then not even 10% of our employees were shareholders.
Our Allianz is resilient, and it is ready to continue growing even in a challenging environment. That is why we've set ourselves an ambitious target for the current fiscal year as well. We are planning an operating profit of EUR 14.8 billion with a range of EUR ±1 billion. That is 4% more compared to last year. Much about the financial figures, but all of that wouldn't be possible, dear shareholders, without satisfied customers.
That is why we've been measuring the Net Promoter Score, so a measure of the customer's loyalty every year since 2016. The latest results impressively show that 3/4 of our companies perform better than their individual competitors. That is a considerable jump of 11 percentage points compared to the previous year.
In addition, 59% of our group companies now have by far the most loyal customers in their respective markets. Our commitment to our customers is the driving force behind these outstanding results, just as in the case of Mrs. Carrel. This is also reflected, by the way, in our brand. In the latest Interbrand brand ranking, we were named the world's number one insurer for the fifth time in a row. Our brand value has exceeded $20 billion for the first time.
Ladies and gentlemen, these results would not be possible without a committed and motivated workforce. Their passion is the key to a first-class customer experience, and that is why we want to become one of the best employers in the world. A central component of this is salary. We reward performance. Moreover, the principle of equal pay for equal work applies regardless of gender.
That should be a given. Today 3/4 of our workforce are working as certified company, and that makes me proud. Of course, we want to have 100% of our companies certified for this. In addition, the topic of learning development is of particular importance, especially in a phase of technological change, because only if you continuously learn, you can succeed in the face of this change.
That is why we invested more than EUR 100 million and 50 hours per employee in this field in the last year. Just to compare, this is almost twice as much as our competitors. Our employees determine the focus of their learning themselves. Some want to get complex issues explained in a simple way. Others want to make better use of artificial intelligence.
All of this makes us more productive, and it gives us more time for what really matters, and that is being close to our customers. In view of these investments, it's no coincidence, as Mr. Diekmann mentioned, that in our last employee survey, we once again reached record results for the fifth time in six years. In the two most important indices in this area in the world. We're at world-class level now, and Allianz is therefore well on the way to being certified globally as a Great Place to Work next year.
This would make us one of the best employers in the world. Already today, one in two Allianz employees works in a company certified in this way, including our Property-Casualty, Life and Health insurance here in Germany. Allianz, due to its size, also has a social responsibility.
That is why we are committed, as you know, to sustainability in all its facets, not just looking at climate change. We support the green transformation of the global economy. We're working together with our partners worldwide to make $9.5 trillion in assets under management CO₂ neutral by 2050, including our own. However, that alone is not enough. We're feeling the effects of climate change day after day here on the ground, whether it's storm, hail, or floods.
Ladies and gentlemen, this is why we have to adapt to climate change. We must take precautions and, for example, do simple things like renewing dikes. We will also have to build differently, and we must no longer build in areas that are threatened by flooding. We also need to make our customers aware of when they can insure themselves against natural hazards. In this way, we want to ensure that our world will still be insurable tomorrow. We're working on this with the entire industry, with all the colleagues together.
Dear shareholders, I have outlined the challenging environment in which Allianz had to prove itself last year and was able to, and I was once again able to present you with a record result. These results are no coincidence. They are the result of a well-functioning strategy, our renewal agenda, and I have already talked about two of its levers to customer centricity and inclusive meritocracy.
Looking ahead to the coming years, I would like to explain to you how we will become more productive in the elements of digital by default and technical excellence and growth engines in order to continue to grow. Let's talk about digitization first. Well, the results are clear.
Since 2016, we have been able to continuously reduce our cost ratio in Property insurance from initially 28% to 24.6% at the end of last year. We also achieved this by harmonizing our products. For example, in personal protection in Germany, in 2019, we set out to develop a comprehensive concept from 11 products.
We closed gaps in the interaction between our products, and we standardized the definitions of coinsured persons and objects, and no surprises was our motto for the new product development. This also enabled us to standardize our processes, and we were able to increase our straight-through processing rate from 75% previously up to 95% now. This means that when a customer buys from us, they immediately receive their documents in an electronic mailbox, and this happens while they're still talking to our agent.
The feedback from our customers shows that we are on the right track. They already rated our service at 4.7 on a five-star scale, compared to 4.4 stars at the start of the journey. By the way, we have also standardized the digital infrastructure of our products. Regardless of whether our customers report a claim to their PrivatSchutz in Germany or to Allianz ULTRA in Italy. The technology behind is and should be the same.
This allows us to take full advantage of our global business model. Ladies and gentlemen, high data quality is extremely important to us. It is the basis for calculating fair premiums, and it determines our competitive position. This is the case. We speak of our technical excellence. Let me give you an insurance example from our health insurance.
In case of small providers and rare diseases, the data quality is often not enough to determine risk appropriate premiums. In some cases, data are missing altogether. In 2022, we therefore began compiling our knowledge about diseases worldwide in a database. Of course, we ensure data protection in the process. In Colombia, for example, we benefit from data from Germany and asthma.
In Germany, we're using knowledge about secondary illness related to malaria. In the future, we want to use this data to provide our customers with even better support in the event of illness. Our aim is to find the right treatment as quickly as possible so that they can get well again as soon as possible. This benefits our customers in two ways. They are spared long medical odysseys and unnecessary costs.
We can already see how powerful this type of steering can be seen in motor insurance. We help our customers get a repair at the best price and the best quality, and this saves up to EUR 1,000 per claim on average. Ladies and gentlemen, we want to continue to grow stronger, profitably also with our commercial business, no matter if it's mid-sized or large corporations. That's why we launched our new Allianz Commercial brand in July 2023.
With this, we offer the entire range of our P&C products under one roof. Our customers and sales partners benefit from a broader range of solutions, and they benefit from a comprehensive advice from just one contact at Allianz. This is well received. We were able to increase the Net Promoter Score among our agents by 16% to 35 points last year.
The operating profit of Allianz Commercial has also risen by an impressive 15% compared with the previous business model. This shows impressively that Allianz Commercial is more than the sum of its parts. Our colleagues in France have also shown how important the customer interface is for our growth. They started generating customer contacts via search engines digitally around three years ago, and they have combined this marketing with expertise because then this will be attributed by AI, and the result is impressive.
The number of digital customer contacts could be increased by 35% or 40%, almost half the cost involved. Today, one in three contacts made digitally leads to a new customer for Allianz. Our brokers decide for themselves whether they want to use the service or not, and if so, they pay for these customer contacts in part.
In this way, we finance this solution together. We will continue this path in the future, not only in France. We will use new technologies and our expertise to win customers for Allianz. Ladies and gentlemen, we want to lead Allianz to even more profitable growth. To achieve this, we will make greater use of new technologies than before.
We will invest the capacities that will become free at the interface with our customers. We want to provide them with even better service in the future and advice, and retain them in Allianz. The expansion and activation of our sales force will play a special role in this. Our Capital Markets Day will take place in 10 December 2024. As part of this, we will give you comprehensive insight into our evolving strategy. We want to stand by our customers, especially in times of uncertainties and change.

content.text:
Moderator
Let me do the housekeeping first and remind you that this conference call is being streamed live on allianz.com and YouTube, and that a recording will be made available shortly after the call. If you want to ask a question after the presentation and you join us via webcast, please click on the Talk Request button at the upper right-hand side of your screen. If you join us via telephone, please press star five. Today's call will be conducted by our CFO, Giulio Terzariol, and our CFO-elect, Claire-Marie Coste-Lepoutre. That's all from my side for now, and with that, I turn the call over to Giulio.
Giulio Terzariol
CFO, Allianz
Thank you, Oliver, and good afternoon and good morning to everybody. Welcome to the call for the Q3 results of Allianz Group. As always, I will start with the nine months view and then Claire-Marie will lead you through the rest of the presentation. If we move to page three, you can see that for the nine months we have a very strong set of results. When you look at the revenue, the revenue up 7%, and that's driven by the Property & Casualty segment and also by the Life segment. In Asset Management, we see a little bit of a negative trend compared to last year, but as you're going to see in a second, in the Q3, we have a positive growth also in Asset Management.
The operating profit is at EUR 11 billion, which is 4% ahead of the last year results and also about 3%-4% ahead of our outlook on a pro rata basis. You can see that in Property & Casualty with a EUR 5.3 billion operating profit; we are in line with our expectation. The combined ratio is slightly more elevated than our target to 93%. On the other side also, we are benefiting from higher investment income. In totality, the operating performance is strong and at the level that we were expecting. In the Life and Health segments, we have an operating profit of EUR 3.8 billion, which is significantly ahead of last year. That's also due to the first time implementation in 2022.
More important, the numbers on the Life side are about a couple of percentage points ahead of our expectations. Also in this segment we are running in a way which is positive compared to what we were expecting at the beginning of the year. The new business margin is stable, a slight increase at a very good level of 5.9%. Also from a new business point of view, we see a good development. In Asset Management, we have an operating profit of EUR 2.2 billion, which is in line with our expectation. Again, we had a quarter with positive inflow, so in total we stand at about EUR 30 billion flows for the first nine months. Net income, or better, core net income is 25% ahead of last year.
Here we need to run a few normalizations. You remember we had the impact of Structured Alpha last year. We had also the gain from the Voya disposal. If we run a couple of normalizations, we get basically back to a growth in core income, which is pretty much consistent with the growth in operating profit. All in all a strong set of results, I will say, across the different segments. As you might recall, last year we had a record profit. Within, with EUR 11 billion of operating profit after nine months, we are well positioned to have, again, in 2023, a strong year and a strong delivery. With that, I will turn it over to Claire-Marie for the quarterly view.
Claire-Marie Coste-Lepoutre
Group CFO, Allianz
Thank you very much, Giulio. Good afternoon, good morning, everyone. I'm very happy to be here today. I will now present to you our Q3 results. Moving on to page five. There you can see that at Q3, we deliver EUR 3.5 billion operating profit, which is a good result in the light of EUR 1.3 billion nat cat load, which is impacting our P&C segment. To put this load into perspective, this is the largest one we have experienced as Allianz Group over the last 10 years, across all quarters. You have to go back to January 2011 to find a similar cat experience. We also have, in particular in this quarter, a negative FX effect, which is impacting our operating profit.
Our operating profit, FX adjusted, will be 10% better compared to last year. Our shareholders' core net income is at EUR 2.1 billion, is basically following the operating profit. The comparison to last year is impacted by the EUR +0.5 billion of positive gains that is coming from the Voya transaction into the quarter. In terms of growth, we experienced a very good top-line growth in Q3 that is stemming from all our segments. This is also a pattern that is accelerated compared to previous quarter. If you look in particular at P&C, you can see there our very strong internal growth that is above 11%. Obviously, for P&C in the combined ratio, you can see the very high effect of the nat cat load.
What I think is very interesting is a very healthy underlying development of our attritional loss ratio, which is as well improving, quarter-on-quarter. That's also a very good sign, I think, in the sense of the actions we have taken to offset the inflationary environment.
Life is as well delivering a very nice growth into the quarter with 8% internal growth at a very good new business margin above 6%, which is as well well ahead of our new business margin target of 5% together with a nice operating profit of EUR 1.3 billion into the quarter. Asset Management is also delivering an operating profit of almost EUR 800 million, double-digit net third party inflows during the quarter, and strong performance fees that are also contributing to the operating profit. Overall at Q3, we see a very healthy and strong underlying business that is impacted by the cat event.
We are very confident we are on the right track for year-end and as well that we have the right base for as we are going to move into next year. If we move to page seven and we have a look at our solvency ratio. Our solvency ratio is at 212 at the end of the quarter, which is up three percentage points versus last quarter. As well, I think it's worth noticing that our sensitivities have slightly reduced versus June to the downward scenario. Overall, I think it's an extremely solid capitalization. This despite our share buyback and the growth we are seeing into the business. This solid capitalization is as well recognized by the rating agencies.
You have certainly noticed that Moody's did upgrade us to Aa2 from Aa3, which is also very good result, I would say on confirming our situation. If we move to next page nine, which is basically presenting the development work of our solvency ratio. What I think is particularly interesting on this page is a very good organic capital generation of 7 percentage points pre-tax and dividend. Life is fully self-financing into the quarter, and only P&C is requiring capital for growth. That's very good development. Overall, I would say on solvency we have no surprises whatsoever in the quarter, and we have an extremely solid base. Let's move now into the P&C segment, and let's look at page 11.
I think this page 11 is actually a very good page. That's a page which is very much in the continuation of the Q2, if you look at it. There we see growth that remains excellent and almost across all our Operating Entities. So that's very solid. What we see as well is a very strong rate change momentum that is continuing quarter-to-quarter. That is really to the credit of our Operating Entities, which have been injecting price actions to offset inflation, and we see that clearly materializing into that page. Let's move now to page 13, and let's have a look at the development of our operating profit.
Operating profit in P&C is at EUR 1.4 billion, which is obviously strongly impacted by the EUR 1.3 billion of nat cat load I was mentioning before. You can see that on the insurance service results, which is down by close to EUR 600 million. But that's also offset partially by the investment results, which is quite supportive of the development. If you have a look at the right-hand side of this page, starting from the bottom, on the insurance revenue, we are EUR 17.5 billion. As I was mentioning, really nice growth, that's well above last year and that's also above last quarter by over 0.6 billion. Our combined ratio clearly is up compared to last year, clearly impacted by nat cat.
If you look at our attritional loss ratio in the underlying, it's 2.4 percentage points better compared to last year and is also better compared to the last two quarters. Again, we see that we are acting on the inflationary trend and that this is showing up into the attritional development too. Year to date, our retail combined ratio is at 95.6, which is a solid performance given the nat cat environment. Commercial, I think continues its very strong trajectory with a combined ratio at 89.7 year to date.
Which is showing not only, I think, the overall environment that is supportive to the commercial business, but as well the actions we have taken in that area. Just maybe before we move on to next page, a brief word on the expense ratio, which is showing higher compared to last year. Actually, the comparison to last year is distorted due to some seasonality effect and also some transitory effect associated to IFRS 17. What I think is important to have in mind is that this 25.1% is in line with previous quarter and is also broadly in line with our expectations in terms of expense ratio.

Director and Equity Analyst, Mediobanca
Excellent, Oliver. Thank you so much for that. And thank you, Claire-Marie. Thank you.
Moderator
Thanks, Vinit.
Claire-Marie Coste-Lepoutre
Group CFO, Allianz
Thank you.
Moderator
All right. We will take the next question from Iain Pearce from Exane. Iain, please go ahead. The line is open.
Iain Pearce
Analyst, Exane
Hi. Thanks for taking my questions. Just two, hopefully quick ones on Life. Firstly, in the Italian business, seems to be really strong new business premium growth. Just wondering what's driving that, and if part of that is sort of recapturing customers that are churning, leading to an elevated number. The second one is just on the new business margins in the US being down year on year. Anything to flag there? Thanks.
Claire-Marie Coste-Lepoutre
Group CFO, Allianz
Sure. On the Italian business, I think, adjusting to the new interest rate environment, our Italian team has injected new product innovation. They have launched three new products for the value channels, which are either a pure unit link or a combination of capital-efficient products together with unit link. That is working very well and is being really welcome by our market, by the market, and, I mean, I would say like appreciated by the agents as well. That's really product innovation, I would say on the Italian side.
New business margin in the US, I think you should not read so much into the year-on-year comparison, in particular for AZ Life. The new business margin for the US business is aiming at delivering the internal rate of return that is needed for our own profitability. You should expect to see some movement there. Overall, AZ Life is returning the expected level of profits to us, adjusted to the environment.
Iain Pearce
Analyst, Exane
Okay, thank you.
Moderator
Thanks, Iain. We will take the next question from Michael Huttner from Berenberg. Michael, please go ahead. Your line is open.
Michael Huttner
Analyst, Berenberg
Thank you very much. I had one number question and two very general. The number question is, can you talk about the net inflows in Life? I think you did broadly mention it, but I probably missed it. I'm sorry. Two more. One is, Allianz normally raises guidance, particularly when the numbers are ahead, and it didn't this time. Maybe you can comment on that. The third one is really for Giulio. I don't know how to say it.
If you think about what is effectively a handover today, and normally I associate a handover and say, "Well, I'd better make sure everything is super conservative." Is there any way that you can show us where that extra conservative might be if there is one? Thank you.
Giulio Terzariol
CFO, Allianz
You're asking me, Michael, to show you the extra conservatives? That's the question?
Michael Huttner
Analyst, Berenberg
Yeah, that's right. Yes.
Giulio Terzariol
CFO, Allianz
Maybe I tell you after January first. I don't know how to answer this question. We'll leave it at that, okay? Yeah. Thank you.
Claire-Marie Coste-Lepoutre
Group CFO, Allianz
Maybe like, let me comment on the outlook. I think overall we are positive that we will end up above the midpoint when it comes to our outlook. Considering the elevated amount of nat cat we see also currently continuing into Q4, we have decided to be cautious because we do not want to set the expectation that we will be significantly ahead of the midpoint, while we might just be moderately ahead of it. That's the main reason why we have kept our outlook stable, unchanged.
On the net, inflows in Life actually year to date our net flows were strongly positive for the U.S., Asia, and LATAM, slightly negative for Spain, and negative by EUR -600 million for Germany, and as well negative for Italy and France. Overall, our net flows will be negative at 9M. I think you should also take into account that traditionally, 9M will be also a moment in time where this is coming across as more negative, because we have less production in Q3 to offset some of the outflows we are seeing. Overall, as I was mentioning, I think we see a good momentum in our Life business.
We are really demonstrating that we have a solid franchise that we are operating across the various regions.
Michael Huttner
Analyst, Berenberg
What is the total net outflow figure?
Moderator
Do we want it for the quarter or for the year to date, Michael? EUR 2 billion. It's EUR 2 billion in that case.
Claire-Marie Coste-Lepoutre
Group CFO, Allianz
It's EUR 2 billion, yeah. Yeah, yeah.
Moderator
By the way, for those who have not spotted it yet, and probably you are part of that group, Michael, we published this number in our supplement.
Michael Huttner
Analyst, Berenberg
That's what I'm looking at. Sorry. I'll look again.
Moderator
It's relatively new, so, you are excused.
Michael Huttner
Analyst, Berenberg
Thank you.
Moderator
All right. I have one last analyst on the line. Cameron, that's you. Sorry, you're last, but definitely not least. The line is open, so please go ahead.
[Analyst]
Analyst
Oh, hey, Oliver. Oh, sorry, all my questions have been answered. I guess no follow-ups for me. Thank you.
Moderator
Perfect. Even better. I see Michael again. Michael, do you have another follow-up question? If yes, please go ahead. Your line is open.
Michael Huttner
Analyst, Berenberg
Can you talk in more? I know you covered Germany in broad terms. Can you talk a little bit more in detail about pricing and claims inflation and all these kind of moving parts in the motor part, in particular in Germany? Just to give you a bit of how I see it, I perceive pricing might just struggle to reach 10%, the renewals which are coming up or which are ongoing, whereas claims inflation is probably just below. My feeling is in motor standalone, you'd probably only return to where you'd like to be in 2025.
Claire-Marie Coste-Lepoutre
Group CFO, Allianz
Yeah. I would say for Germany, we would expect to be where we want to be in 2025. In terms of combined ratio performance, we have observed in Germany overall a bit higher inflation effects compared to what we had anticipated initially. We have taken rate actions, and we have acted structurally over the portfolio. You can see that with our year to date rate momentum, which is above 6% for Germany overall.
Now to your specific point around pricing for Germany, I think we our operating entity our German operating entity is very well advanced in terms of technical excellence. We have pricing models which are very precise and capable of also estimating what we would need to have in the given also as an example in own business given the localization of the business and so on and so forth. Then obviously there is a difference between the in-force book and the new business. We are slowly converging and managing the pricing level across the portfolio.
I think we are maneuvering the inflationary environment in a very good way at our German entity. I would expect that to show up into our performance definitely towards 2025.
Michael Huttner
Analyst, Berenberg
Is there hope that we might get a double-digit rate rise in motor at renewals just now? Or, sorry to be so-
Moderator
Michael, I can do this. This is Oliver. I can give you a real life example. My premium went up by 7% and I never drive. I mean, I park my car all day long. You can trust that everybody, all the customers that we have that do drive their car from time to time, got a double-digit rate increase already now.
Michael Huttner
Analyst, Berenberg
Brilliant. Fantastic. That was the answer I was looking for. Thank you so much. Thank you and good luck both of you. All three of you, sorry.
Claire-Marie Coste-Lepoutre
Group CFO, Allianz
Thank you.
Moderator
All right. Thanks everybody for your contributions. That's the end of our analyst call. We say goodbye and thank you to everybody. Before I leave, let me just remind you that we have the upcoming Inside Allianz Series in London in two weeks time. This event will be joined by both by Claire-Marie and by Giulio. If you want to say goodbye to Giulio and hello to Claire-Marie, that's the perfect opportunity, and I hope we all see you there in two weeks time in London. Thank you and goodbye from my side.
Claire-Marie Coste-Lepoutre
Group CFO, Allianz
Thank you. Bye-bye.
Giulio Terzariol
CFO, Allianz
Goodbye, guys. See you in London. Bye.
Claire-Marie Coste-Lepoutre
Group CFO, Allianz
Bye. Bye-bye.

content.text:
Giulio Terzariol
CFO, Allianz SE
Value swings for the swings on assets which are marked at fair value, where we don't have an offset coming from the liability side. Also, we adjust for the PGAAP adjustment, which are in any case in our case a very small amount. I'd like to draw your attention to the core net income, because that's also the way we are going to monitor our performance. The primary KPIs are going to be clearly operating profit as always, and then we're going to focus on the core net income. All in all, I would say nothing is the major change on the aggregate level. If we go now to page , look at the P&C business. Here you see EUR 600 million more of operating profit.
Basically, the additional operating profit is coming from the net effect of discounting and unwinding. I know that you know the mechanics by now, clearly in the course of 2022, since rates have gone up, we get a higher benefit for discounting compared to the unwinding, which is based on the interest rate level of the preceding years. As you know, the preceding years had a very low interest rates environment. You see this geography also reflected in the insurance service results, which is going up compared to the old system because of the discounting. Then the operating investment results is going down compared to the old system because of the unwinding effect. The combined ratio is lower under the new methodology. That's because of the discounting impact.
Structurally, if you remove the discounting impact from the combined ratio, the combined ratio has a tendency to be higher, and that's because it's based on a gross basis, when we look at the denominator instead of being based on a net basis. That's in short the story on the P&C side. Net impact of discounting is positive in 2022, due to the rate environment. Now we come to page 9 on the development on the life business. In this case, you see that the operating profit was substantially lower. We are doing here normalization. We are basically normalizing for the hedge results of Allianz Life.
The point here is when Allianz Life is doing the hedges, they are doing the hedges also based on the accounting that is in place, and clearly the hedges were calibrated last year to the IFRS 4 accounting. The new accounting, clearly, that we need to implement retrospectively has a different sensitivity, and that's the reason why we got an accounting mismatch. If we had had this kind of accounting, the IFRS 17 accounting also last year, our hedging program would have been different. On top of that, also, we refined the methodology of how we run the IFRS 17 calculation, but we implemented this new methodology only in 2023 and not in 2022. That's also leading to a part of this normalization that we do.
All in all, when you normalize the numbers, you get basically to an operating profit, which is broadly in line with the old basis. When you look then at the net income is absolutely in line with the old basis, and that's because we have some geographic issue between the operating profit and the below the line item. The bottom line is in the new representation reality, when you look at the net income or core net income, but for the life business is more or less the same, you're not going to see a much different number compared to the old system.
Now we come to page 11, and that's about the reconciliation between what we call the comprehensive shareholder capital, which is the sum of the shareholder equity in the CSM and the Solvency II own funds. Here we are removing the usual suspects, like the tier two subordinate liability, the foreseeable dividend distribution. We are removing the items which are by definition different methodological approach. What is relevant in reality in this slide is the last item, which is other. As you see, there is basically no major difference once we remove all the other items between the comprehensive shareholder capital and the Solvency II own funds. The message in this slide is basically that the two bases of valuation are broadly very consistent from a technical point of view.
With that, we come to the IFRS 9 and 17 leverage. This is the way we are looking at leverage, which is basically the comprehensive capital in relation to the amount of debt that we are holding. Based on this new methodology, the leverage ratio is about 24%, which is lower compared to the leverage ratio based on the old system. We don't know yet what rating agencies are going to do, and by the way, rating agencies are going to follow different approaches, but we think that's also a way to look at the leverage ratio. That's also, I believe, a way to look at the leverage ratio, which is going to be pretty standard also in the industry.
That was just, you know, a very short update on the numbers for 2022 based on the new system. I believe the best way to familiarize with the new account is to speak about current numbers. As I said, also in the press call, no matter what kind of accounting we are using. We are going to provide clearly good results, and the reason is the underlying performance and the fundamentals of the business are very strong. Any accounting system is going to reflect this strong performance. When we look at the Q1, we had a very good start into 2023. From a revenue point of view, we continue to see strong revenue in property casualty, double-digit growth.
In the case of Life/Health and Asset Management, revenue is subdued, but that's not clearly a surprise considering that there is still some instability in the market. The operating profit is ahead of last year, but also, more important, is ahead of the outlook. If you take our outlook divided by four, we are basically 5% ahead compared to that number, and this is coming both from Property-Casualty and from the Life/Health business. In the case of Asset Management, we are a little bit behind the outlook divided by four, but that's normal because we are going to get the performance fees at the end of the year. Also in the case of Asset Management, we are positive that we can achieve our outlook for 2023. The operational KPIs are going in the right direction.
Basically, if you take out the cost-income ratio for Asset Management, you're going to see an improvement in the operational KPIs. We saw also positive flows at AGI and PIMCO in Q1. The core net income is at EUR 2.2 billion. Here we have also the impact from the potential disposal of Allianz in Lebanon. If you adjust for this impact, which is an accounting impact, it's not really an economic impact, the shareholder core net income will be north of EUR 2.3 billion. If you analyze the number, you get to EUR 9.4 billion of core income for the year, which is also what will be an expectation for this new KPI.
All in all, very strong performance on the operational side, and also when you look at the operating profit, especially once you adjust it for the accounting impact coming from the potential Lebanon transaction. What was positive is the development of the solvency ratio, 206. If you look at the sensitivities are pretty much unchanged compared to the sensitivities that we had at the end of the year. On Wednesday night, we announced the buyback, so we continue to deploy capital, which is clearly a sign of the comfort that we have with our capital level and also with our clear liquidity situation. From that point of view, we continue to create profit, capital, liquidity, and that's also very important, we continue to deploy capital.
If you go to page 21 on the evolution of the Solvency II, basically the capital generation is in line with our expectation. The markets have been benign, so we benefited from the market environment a bit. Then also what is important under capital management action, you see the deduction for the accrual of the dividends, but also there was about 1 percentage point, little bit less than that, of impact on the solvency ratio because of an investment that we did in Innovation Group. We continue to invest basically in capabilities that should support our technical excellence on the property casualty side. All in all, 206 solvency ratio, if you adjust for the buyback that we announced on Wednesday, the number is very robust at 2.2.
Now we come to the segment view, starting from P&C. Overall you see a very good growth rate of double-digit 11%, and also you can see that overall there is a good growth rate at most entities. Also, what is important, the change in renewal is pretty solid and accelerating compared to the change in renewal that we had also during the course of 2022. You see a constant acceleration over time. From that point of view, what this slide is showing is that we have been reacting strongly to the challenge of inflation, and this also bodes well clearly for the operating performance.
When we look at the operating performance from a bottom line point of view, you can see that our operating profit at page 25 has gone up by about EUR 350 million. The improvement in the operating profit is coming from the so-called insurance service results, which is, if you want, something similar to the old underwriting results. This is explained by the improvement of the combined ratio by about 2 percentage points. Clearly, in the quarter, we benefited from a lower amount on net cat compared to last year, but also you can see that our non-cat has been very conservative. All in all, we were extremely happy with the performance of our entity, and we didn't really push this number, so that's very important.
91.9 is 1 percentage point better compared to the number that we put forward as an outlook for 2023. We are running stronger than that, and we feel very good about the underlying performance behind this number when we think also about the quality, clearly, of the number, because one thing is the number and the level, one thing is the quality, and the quality is really good. We can see this reflected also on the performance by OE at page 27. You see a lot of good combined ratios, so a lot of our companies are performing at combined ratio, which are under the new method below 90%. I would also like to highlight that in Brazil, Latin America, we are making good progress.
In Spain, considering the market environment, we have also solid performance. In the UK, I would say the numbers are good considering the market environment. We benefited from lower Nat Cat. From that point of view in the UK, the situation is still a little bit more complicated than in other countries, as you see also from the disclosure of the competitors. Overall, we are taking strong action. When you look at the total portfolio, we have really a very strong performance across a lot of entities. We are also very confident that we are continuing to see strong numbers in the following quarters. Now we come to the investment income, page 29.
It might look surprising that the operating investment results goes down, but in reality, with the new method, we have a situation where the accretion or the interest rate is going somehow to compensate for the increase in investment income coming from clearly the higher interest rate environment. So from that point of view, we need to start thinking differently about the evolution of this KPI, which is going to be more flattish year over year. In our case then, in this case, we have a drop compared to last year just because last year we had positive FX effects in the valuation results and others.
The main message here, it's kind of a trend that you should expect to stay at that level based on the old system, because I'm sure the question will come, what would have been the number? The number would have been north of EUR 800 million. So again, might look surprising, but in reality it's not a surprise at all, and that's very consistent with our plan. All in all, 1.9 almost of operating profit in Property-Casualty. If you remember, our outlook was EUR 7 billion. If you annualize 1.9, you get to something close. If you annualize the number, you get something like EUR 7.5 billion. We are definitely ahead of our outlook for the year.
We expect also that we will continue to see this kind of run rate in the following quarters. Now we come to life. On the Life business, page 31, when we look at the production, we see there is a drop in production of about 12%. Here, we need to consider that we had the impact of the discounting, which is more a technical impact. If you remove that effect, you get to a growth rate of -6%, which is clearly much better than -12%. It's not surprising that in this situation where there is still some uncertainty, the production of unit-linked or of single premium is going to be lower. On the other side, the new business margin is going up, so we have very strong new business margin.
This is a pre-tax number that's important. If you do an after-tax number, you're going to get closer to the 4% that you were used to see based on the Solvency II approach. What is important, we are seeing an increase in the new business margin. When you put together the production evolution, the new business margin evolution, you get then to a very new business of more than EUR 1 billion, which is relatively stable compared to the prior period, and more importantly, is also a healthy level of new business. At page 33, we are showing now the evolution of the CSM, and we like to focus on the so-called normalized CSM growth, which is the sum of CSM at inception, which is basically the CSM on new business.
We have an expectation of a certain growth of the CSM, and then we have the CSM release into the profit. We like to look at the combination of these three figures. In our case, we have a growth rate for the quarter of about 1%. If you annualize that number, you get basically to an annualized growth of 4%. Why we like to look at this number? Because to a certain degree, there is high correlation between the growth in the CSM and the future growth in the operating profit. Overall, I would say a good growth for the CSM. We see here a comment on the non-economic variances and assumption change. The EUR 1 billion is a large number, but that's all driven by a change in the way we are including Mexico in our CSM.
Basically, we are excluding Mexico, the Mexican business from the CSM, because this is not necessarily a business that has to be accounted under IFRS 9 and IFRS 17. If you adjust for that change in approach, the economic variances, the non-economic variances, and assumption changes are a very small number of about EUR 200 million. With that, we can go to the next slide, which is on the operating profit drivers. This, the operating profit for us, is a bit ahead of our expectation, which is a good thing. At the same time, it's very much consistent, I would say, when you look at the single drivers with the expectation that we set when we had the call in December.
If you go back and look at the document, you're going to see that the single drivers are within the ranges or the expectation that we gave you. Clearly a number that tends to be more volatile. We said that from the very beginning, it's the operating investment results. It was extremely volatile last year because of this accounting mismatch I was referring to due to the first time implementation for Allianz Life. Definitely that number is too low compared to a normal expectation. On the other side, the first quarter 2023 number might be a little bit on the high end of the potential range. But as you understand, it's also a new calculation for us.
In order to be able to establish what is a run rate on this dimension, we will need a little bit more experience. The bottom line is strong performance from the Life segment. Again, you can see that under the new methodology, we are recording a good profitability basically at the same level you were used to in the older system. There is a KPI that we are not showing anymore, which is the difference between the current yield and the guaranteed evolution. If you remember, the spread was about 230 basis points. Last year, this number is going up by about 20 basis points as we speak because of the production that we are putting our system and because of the higher rates.
From that point of view, there is a nice trend underlying clearly the solidity of our life business. At page 37, we are showing the numbers for the selected entities. I will say that, when you look at the normalized CSM growth, it's pretty consistent across the different entities. When you look at the operating performance, you can see also a good level of operating performance. No major surprises, no surprises compared to what you were used to before. On that one, I would also say for the majority of the OEs, you can see there is a tight relationship between the CSM release and the operating profit. There are two exceptions. One is Italy and one is CE, Eastern Europe, Central and Eastern Europe.
Here you see that the operating profit is higher compared to the CSM release because some of the business in Italy and CE is not accounting for under IFRS 17. Bottom line, strong results on the life side with good new business margin and also an operating profit, which is slightly ahead of our expectation. Also from a quality point of view, you can see the consistency between what we told you a few months ago and what is happening right now. Now we can go into asset management, and I will skip directly to page 41. Here you can see that the third party assets under management went up by about 2%, and this is driven on the one side also from the movement of the markets net of the effects.
There is also a contribution coming from flows. As we always said, if the situation is stabilizing, we are going to see flows coming back. Especially at the beginning of the year, the situation on the capital market was more benign. This explains also the positive flows that we saw at PIMCO. From that point of view, there is a reversal of the trend that we saw in the course of 2022. At page 43 on the revenue, it's not surprising the revenues are down. That's a consequence of the development of 2022. What is positive, you can see that the fee margin is going up. That's the case for PIMCO. In the case of PIMCO and also for the segment, because PIMCO clearly represents the majority of the segment.
In the case of AGI, you see fee margin decreasing. That has to do with the Voya transaction. On the other side, we need also to recognize that the expenses are not there anymore. In reality, from a profitability point of view, the transaction of Voya is more or less of a wash, which is better compared to the initial expectation that we had. Now we come to page 45. On the operating profit evolution, the operating profit is down versus last year, but that's in line with our expectation. If you remember for the year 2023, we have an outlook of EUR 3 billion. If you take the quarterly number and you annualize that number, you get to EUR 2.9 billion.
If you think that we get the performance fees at the end of the year, it means that we are well on track to achieve that target if markets are stable or not completely erratic by the end of the year. Bottom line, solid results in asset management in line with expectation. Also, we saw flows coming back in the first quarter and also year to date. Page 47. On the corporate segment, I would say it's in line with expectation, a little bit better compared to last year, and that's because of some more profit coming from our banking operations in Italy. Then at page 49 on the net income, and look at the non-operating items, you see that the realized gains and losses are lower compared to last year.
Last year, in Q1, we had the disposal of a participation, and also we had some realized gains on bonds. On the other side, you see that the restructuring expenses are lower compared to Q1 last year, where we had also the restructuring coming partially from the Voya transaction, and from some restructuring in Germany. What you see here is this volatility coming from the assets measured at fair value. This is also the volatility that we remove below the line. It's not one to one. There are some elements that we are not removing from this line item, but the majority of this volatility is removed in the definition of core net income.
All in all, EUR 2.2 billion core net income. I said before, if you remove Lebanon and you annualize the number, it's a strong core net income of EUR 9.4 billion, as a sort of what could be an expectation, a normalized level for the year. Now we come to the last slide. Overall, again, a strong set of results. I would really say excellent start into the year with strong operating performance, I would say, across the board. We are 5% ahead of our outlook divided by four. We also see good momentum, so we believe we are going to carry this good momentum in Q2 and also in the remainder of the year. Also, we announced a buyback just the other day of EUR 1.5 billion.
We are also, at the same time, investing in the business, as I was saying before. I would say that we are very pleased with the results, but especially we are pleased with the momentum that we see flowing through our businesses. With that, I would like to open up to your questions.
Oliver Schmidt
Head of Investor Relations, Allianz SE
All right. Thanks, Giulio. Thank you for your presentation. We now will be happy to answer your questions, and we will take the first question from Andrew Sinclair, Bank of America. Andrew, your line is open. Please go ahead.
Andrew Sinclair
Head of Insurance Equity Research, Bank of America
Thank you, and good afternoon, everyone. Three from me, please, and thanks for all the new disclosure as well. First is on the P&C business. You talked about the quality of results, and I feel you've kind of been making a similar message for the last few quarters about booking the current year conservatively when you're getting so much investment income, et cetera. Without detailed reserve triangles, how can we really see that that prudence is being built? Where can you give us some numbers just to provide some comfort about the extra prudence going into reserves? That's question one. Second question was on capital return. Why was EUR 1.5 billion the right number? Solvency ratio is still over 200% post the buyback.
Just thoughts on what could come next. I realize you just announced one, but what are the thoughts on further buybacks versus M&A? Third was just on Life. You talked about the hedges in the US, and they're gonna be adjusted for the new accounting, particularly in the US. Just sounded a little bit strange to me. I mean, I'd have thought hedging would be focused on the economics rather than the accounting. Can you just tell us a little bit more about what hedge changes you've been making there and how we can feel comfortable that those economics are well hedged? Thanks.
Giulio Terzariol
CFO, Allianz SE
No, thank you for the question. Starting from the first one, which is about the prudency and how you can get comfort with the prudency. The one way, in reality, one way to do is you spend a lot of quality time with the chief actuary. You go through all the numbers, and then you're going to get the confidence. The other way to do it is just look at our track record. You can also see when net cat are lower, the runoff is magically lower. When net cat are higher, you see that there is more runoff coming through. We are managing to an outcome. At the end of the day, you can see that over time we have been extremely consistent. The proof point is just look at the consistency on how we deliver numbers. Just go back, do some analysis.
You're going to see lower net cat. Automatically, you see a little bit more runoff. You see also less runoff. You see also the attritional loss ratio tends to be a little bit higher and vice versa. This is a sign, clearly, that we have a lot of balance sheet strength. Also that when we have situation like this, where the net cat are lower, we are going to use this situation clearly to also even further strengthen the balance sheet, let's put it this way. We are managing to an outcome. We said that, think about 2023, the combined ratio we said 93%.
Now we are running 91.9% with a high quality, and we can assure you we are not sweating to achieve this 91.9% combined ratio. The other way is you need really to spend a lot of time with our actuaries, but we are not going to give you access to our actuaries. Really, seriously, look at the numbers over time, put the numbers down in a table, and you are definitely going to see this kind of pattern. Also, just look at the stated combined ratio. We are speaking of, in general, very strong numbers. Also, look at the combined ratio across the entities.
You also don't see, that's also a sign, you don't see a big dispersion of combined ratio, where maybe a couple of entities are posting 80 combined ratio to offset for a lot of businesses performing maybe not so good. In our case, you see rather a lot of companies performing very good, and then maybe you might have a couple of companies having a little bit of a more elevated combined ratio. That's also something I do. I always, you know, when I look at other companies, I always look whether the combined ratio is equally distributed between the entities, or you have somebody carry more of the weight. I would say in our situation, you can see that there is a lot of quality across the board. That's on the combined ratio message.

Thank you. At first, following up on what Giulio just said on the outlook. In what extent does this change to IFRS 9 and 17 have consequences for your outlook? There are some competitors that gave more or less concrete number. How big the gap is between the current system and the future system. What components does IFRS 17 have in your outlook? The other one, on what Oliver Bäte said, I remember in or shortly after the COVID outbreak, you said Allianz would probably need 30% less real estate for housing your employees.
Has your view changed on that, or what's the policy regarding home office and all the like? Will we be back to...
